THE FIELD GUIDE

Understand the ideas.
Then put them to the test.

Start with gravity, explore extreme objects, or follow energy from one nucleus to another.

01 / GRAVITY

Orbits are
continuous free fall.

A planet moves sideways while gravity bends its path. A circular orbit needs just the right speed for its distance and the central mass.

Understand the balance +

For a circular orbit around a dominant central mass, v = √(GM/r). A larger mass requires a higher circular speed at the same radius. Without that extra speed, a formerly circular orbit can become elliptical.

Try the gravity lab ↗
02 / EXTREME OBJECTS

A star’s ending.
A new kind of beginning.

Some massive stellar cores become neutron stars. Others collapse into black holes. Their small sizes and large masses make gravity extreme.

Look closer +

A neutron star has a material surface; a black hole has an event horizon. A pulsar is a rotating neutron star whose beams can sweep across Earth like a lighthouse.

Explore compact objects ↗
03 / ENERGY

Small particles.
Enormous possibilities.

Fusion joins light nuclei; fission splits a heavy nucleus. Energy is released when the products have less total rest mass than the inputs.

Follow the energy +

The mass difference appears as energy: E = Δmc². Nucleon number and electric charge stay balanced in the reaction examples in this lab. The Sun mainly uses the proton–proton chain; the D–T example shown here is a different fusion reaction.

FROM AN IDEA TO AN EXPERIMENT

Keep asking “what if?”

01

Start with one question.

What changes when mass increases? What stays the same when a nucleus splits?

02

Change one variable.

Keep the other settings fixed so you can connect a change to its result.

03

Explain what you saw.

Compare your prediction with the result. Check the model’s assumptions before drawing a conclusion.
